{{See also|Time complexity#Sub-exponential time}}

A growth rate is said to be '''infra-exponential''' or '''subexponential''' if it is dominated by all [[exponential growth]] rates, however great the [[doubling time]]. A [[continuous function]] with infra-exponential growth rate will have a [[Fourier transform]] that is a Fourier [[hyperfunction]].<ref>[https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Fourier_hyperfunction Fourier hyperfunction] in the [[Encyclopedia of Mathematics]]
</ref>

Examples of subexponential growth rates arise in the [[analysis of algorithms]], where they give rise to [[Time complexity#Sub-exponential time|sub-exponential time complexity]], and in the [[Growth rate (group theory)|growth rate of groups]], where a subexponential growth rate implies that a group is [[amenable group|amenable]].

A positive-valued, unbounded [[probability distribution]] <math>\cal D</math> may be called '''subexponential''' if its tails are heavy enough so that{{r|GK|at=Definition 1.1}}
:<math>\lim_{x\to+\infty} \frac{{\Bbb P}(X_1+X_2>x)}{{\Bbb P}(X>x)}=2,\qquad X_1, X_2, X\sim {\cal D},\qquad X_1, X_2 \hbox{ independent.}</math>
See {{slink|Heavy-tailed distribution|Subexponential distributions}}.  Contrariwise, a [[random variable]] may also be called '''subexponential''' if [[subexponential distribution (light-tailed)|its tails are sufficiently light to fall off at an exponential or faster rate]].
